Suspended animation

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Saving lives through suspended animation

Summary:
NEITHER dead or alive, knife-wound or gunshot victims will be cooled down and placed in suspended animation, as a groundbreaking emergency technique is tested out for the first time.

Further information:
GUNSHOT VICTIMS TO BE SUSPENDED BETWEEN LIFE AND DEATH
Doctors will try to save the lives of patients with knife or gunshot wounds by placing them in suspended animation, buying time to fix their injuries
No heartbeat, no hope?
No heartbeat, no hope?
NEITHER dead or alive, knife-wound or gunshot victims will be cooled down and placed in suspended animation, as a groundbreaking emergency technique is tested out for the first time. Surgeons are now on call at the UPMC Presbyterian Hospital in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to perform the operation, which will buy doctors time to fix injuries that would otherwise be lethal. “We are suspending life, but we don’t like to call it suspended animation because it sounds like science fiction,” says Samuel Tisherman, a surgeon at the hospital, who is leading the trial. “So we call it emergency preservation and resuscitation.” The technique involves replacing all of a patient’s blood with a cold saline solution, which rapidly cools the body and stops almost all cellular activity. “If a patient comes to us two hours after dying you can’t bring them back to life. But if they’re dying and you suspend them, you have a chance to bring them back after their structural problems have been fixed,” says surgeon Peter Rhee at the University of Arizona in Tucson, who helped develop the technique.
The benefits of cooling, or induced hypothermia, have been known for decades. At normal body temperature – around 37 °C – cells need a regular oxygen supply to produce energy. When the heart stops beating, blood no longer carries oxygen to cells. Without oxygen the brain can only survive for about 5 minutes before the damage is irreversible.
However, at lower temperatures, cells need less oxygen because all chemical reactions slow down. This explains why people who fall into icy lakes can sometimes be revived more than half an hour after they have stopped breathing.
Just before heart and brain surgery, doctors sometimes lower body temperature using ice packs, and by circulating the blood through an external cooling system. This can give them up to 45 minutes in which to stop blood flow and perform surgery. However, the cooling process takes time and can only be done with careful planning and preparation.
When someone reaches an emergency department with a traumatic gunshot injury or stab wound, slow cooling isn’t an option. Often their heart has stopped beating due to extreme blood loss, giving doctors only minutes to stop the bleeding and restart the heart. Even if the bleeding can be stopped, it’s not like filling up an empty gas tank. Resuscitation exposes the body to a sudden onslaught of oxygen, which can cause tissues to release chemicals that damage cells and cause fatal “reperfusion” injuries.
Finding ways to cool the body until it reaches a state of suspended animation – where people are not alive but not yet dead – could give doctors more time in an emergency.
The technique was first demonstrated in pigs in 2000 by Rhee and his colleagues. The animals were sedated and a massive haemorrhage induced, to mimic the effect of multiple gunshot wounds. Their blood was drained and replaced by either a cold potassium or saline solution, rapidly cooling the body to around 10 °C. After the injuries were treated, the animals were gradually warmed up as the solution was replaced with blood.
Vital signs
The pig’s heart usually started beating again by itself, although some pigs needed a jump-start. There was no effect on physical or cognitive function (Surgery, doi.org/dvhdzs).
“After we did those experiments, the definition of ‘dead’ changed,” says Rhee. “Every day at work I declare people dead. They have no signs of life, no heartbeat, no brain activity. I sign a piece of paper knowing in my heart that they are not actually dead. I could, right then and there, suspend them. But I have to put them in a body bag. It’s frustrating to know there’s a solution.”
“I sign a piece of paper knowing in my heart that they are not actually dead. It’s frustrating”
That solution will be put to the test in humans for the first time. A final meeting this week will ensure that a team of doctors is fully prepared to try it. Then all they have to do is wait for the right patient to arrive.
That person will have suffered a cardiac arrest after a traumatic injury, and will not have responded to attempts to start their heart. When this happens, every member of Tisherman’s team will be paged. “The patient will probably have already lost about 50 per cent of their blood and their chest will be open,” he says. The team sees one of these cases each month. Their chance of survival is less than 7 per cent.
The first step is to flush cold saline through the heart and up to the brain – the areas most vulnerable to low oxygen. To do this, the lower region of their heart must be clamped and a catheter placed into the aorta – the largest artery in the body – to carry the saline. The clamp is later removed so the saline can be artificially pumped around the whole body. It takes about 15 minutes for the patient’s temperature to drop to 10 °C. At this point they will have no blood in their body, no breathing, and no brain activity. They will be clinically dead.
In this state, almost no metabolic reactions happen in the body, so cells can survive without oxygen. Instead, they may be producing energy through what’s called anaerobic glycolysis. At normal body temperatures this can sustain cells for about 2 minutes. At low temperatures, however, glycolysis rates are so low that cells can survive for hours. The patient will be disconnected from all machinery and taken to an operating room where surgeons have up to 2 hours to fix the injury. The saline is then replaced with blood. If the heart does not restart by itself, as it did in the pig trial, the patient is resuscitated. The new blood will heat the body slowly, which should help prevent any reperfusion injuries.
The technique will be tested on 10 people, and the outcome compared with another 10 who met the criteria but who weren’t treated this way because the team wasn’t on hand. The technique will be refined then tested on another 10, says Tisherman, until there are enough results to analyse.
“We’ve always assumed that you can’t bring back the dead. But it’s a matter of when you pickle the cells,” says Rhee.
“Until now we had always assumed that you can’t bring people back from the dead”
Getting this technique into hospitals hasn’t been easy. Because the trial will happen during a medical emergency, neither the patient nor their family can give consent. The trial can only go ahead because the US Food and Drug Administration considers it to be exempt from informed consent. That’s because it will involve people whose injuries are likely to be fatal and there is no alternative treatment. The team had to have discussions with groups in the community and place adverts in newspapers describing the trial. People can opt out online. So far, nobody has.

Tisherman says he eventually hopes to extend the technique to other conditions.
For now, suspended animation is limited to a few hours. But that’s not to say that more lengthy suspension isn’t possible (see “Will human hibernation ever happen“).
“We’re trying to save lives, not pack people off to Mars,” says Tisherman. “Can we go longer than a few hours with no blood flow? I don’t know. Maybe years from now someone will have figured out how to do it, but it will certainly take time.”

Press Release:


Humans in Suspended Animation
No pulse, no hope? Remarkable scientific advances are giving knife-wound and gunshot victims a real chance at the proverbial nine lives. A ground-breaking emergency technique cools down injured people and places them in a state of so-called suspended animation (neither dead nor alive) and could buy doctors critical time needed to patch the holes and save lives. Carte Blanche meets the doctors duelling with death—and winning.


Script:


V/O:
24 hours ago this animal was dead. It had no heartbeat…. it did not breathe…. it had no blood… in fact, its veins were filled with cold salt water… and there was no brain activity.

But then this team of researchers brought it back to life.
Peter Rhee:
What we had traditionally thought of as being dead, when your heart stopped moving, when your brain is not getting any oxygen and we’ve taken all the blood out of your body -- that is reversible.
V/O:
We met trauma surgeon Prof Peter Rhee at The University of Arizona in Tucson. Having served as a battlefield casualty physician in Afghanistan and Iraq, he is now part of a team that has developed a ground-breaking protocol to keep recently deceased animals in suspended animation for hours before reversing their death—without any negative side effects.
Sam Tisherman
We can look at the brain function. We have various ways of testing to see that they’re acting like normal animals. And we found that with an hour they’re normal. A lot of them are normal even with two hours of no blood flow.
V/O:
Prof Sam Tisherman is a trauma specialist at The University of Maryland’s School of Medicine. In collaboration with Peter Rhee, he is about to embark on a clinical trial attempting to bring people back from the dead in a similar fashion.

Their work was sparked by their experiences as surgeons treating gunshot and stabbing victims in trauma units in American cities and in theatres of war.
Peter:
In the US we have a hundred thousand people a year that get shot. So we actually had this need, not just in the military. But in our country in the civilian world, people come into us dead from being shot all the time.
V/O:
Peter has video-taped many of the cases he has treated. Both he and Sam have time and again witnessed stab wound and gunshot victims come into the emergency room with cardiac arrest caused by severe blood loss—making it impossible to save them.
Sam:
The problem that we face is that often times the Injuries are fixable. The problem is we’re racing against the clock. And we can’t fix injuries, get the bleeding stopped before it is too late.
LINK:
This means that surgeons often do not have enough time to repair the injuries that is causing the severe bleeding. This leads to irreversible brain and organ damage.
V/O:
Trauma surgeons are currently forced to resort to drastic measures to try and save patients. This is one of Peter’s cases.
Peter:
So they are doing CPR on that patient as he comes in, because he is already dead. And so if we don’t do anything he’s going to stay dead. But in this patient we were able to quickly open his chest, we do that without any anaesthesia or any prepping because you are already dead.
V/O:
This is called an emergency resuscitative thoracotomy. Doctors clamp the aorta to preserve blood for the brain and heart and then try to repair the wounds.
Peter:
If it works you survive, if it doesn’t work we haven’t lost anything. This is us repairing the hole in his heart.
V/O:
This man survived. However, the survival rate using this last resort technique in military and civilian settings is very, very low.
Sam:
Peter Rhee did a review some fifteen years ago and the total was around seven percent. So it’s pretty bad, we can’t save many of them. In theory, if you had something novel, something new you could do, you might have been able to save some time to save them. What we do now doesn’t work, we’re losing patients daily and we got to try something different.
V/O:
Something different would be finding a way to suspend life to give surgeons more time to repair the injuries causing the bleeding.

And the only way to buy more time is to find a way to protect the brain against the effects of blood loss.

Both Sam and Peter have interacted with Dr Peter Safar. He is the man who developed CPR in the nineteen fifties and is known as the father of critical care. He once suggested a revolutionary way to go about protecting the brain – through hypothermia. This became the basis for what Peter and Sam have been working on for the last decade and a half.
Peter:
Instead of trying to fix the hole that was bleeding, can we buy ourselves maybe an hour of time by preserving the brain, by cooling it real fast and then while we are fixing the holes that are bleeding, bring the patient back up later on over slower time periods?
V/O:
Buying time by cooling a patient down made sense to them. It is a known fact that when the brain is cooled down, brain damage is limited.
LINK:
There are also many instances of people who drown in ice cold water, but then go on to survive the ordeal with little or no brain damage.
V/O:
Brain and heart surgeons also cool patients down as part of procedures that require that blood circulation be stopped for some time. Hypothermia seems to be the critical factor.
Sam:
Hypothermia basically affects every cell, every enzyme in the body and basically slows everything down. So cells require less energy, organs require less energy and thereby the need for oxygen, the need for blood flow that brings oxygen to the tissues goes down with the temperature. So the lower the temperature, the less oxygen is needed.
LINK:
This meant that if they could find a way to cool a victim down rapidly, the all the vital organs, including the brain, would require much less oxygen.
V/O:
And at these very low temperatures the brain can survive—even without oxygen—for some time. The big question became: could they cool somebody down rapidly in a trauma situation?

After obtaining permission to carry out a study on pigs they were able to carefully operate on the animals and determine whether their unusual methods would have the expected results.

This pig’s heart has just stopped beating. To cool the whole body down rapidly they pump a freezing cold salt water solution directly into the animal’s aorta.
Peter:
When we get into the blood stream and we pump and infuse cold saline into the body, we can cool every cell in the brain down very, very quickly.
LINK:
The cold saline solution replaced the blood of the animals and this lowered their body temperatures quickly and drastically.
Peter:
These were animals that were technically dead for anything from an hour to three hours. They had no blood in their body, they were at ten degrees.
V/O:
This very low temperature ensured that the animals sustained no brain damage and bought the surgeons more than enough time to fix all the damaged vessels that caused the bleeding.

Once repairs had been finalised, they connected the animals to a heart lung machine and slowly warmed them up by replacing the cold saline with blood.

Their first attempt was utterly nerve wracking.
Peter:
I’ll never forget that day. I’ll never forget that day. I remember distinctly we were all in the laboratory. There was a whole bunch of doctors and nurses and people in there. And when I warmed that pig back up and the heart started moving after it had been dead for well over an hour and a half. With no blood, cold, full of potassium solutions. But when that heart started to beat back up again, I could feel the hair on my neck going up and I almost felt like what Frankenstein would have felt like when he was doing his experiments.
Link:
And what is more, none of the animals sustained brain damage.
Sam:
So the function seems to be normal. We can actually look at their brains. We can have pathologists look to see if there is any brain damage. So as best as we could tell from the function, the pathologist says they look normal.
Peter:
So that where we are at now. We are at a phase where the science is good enough that we think we can try it in humans.
LINK:
Sam and his team have applied to the FDA to conduct human trials on 10 people in Pittsburgh. The application has been approved and trials are set to start very soon.
Sam:
Right now we just want to show that is can work. If we can show it works in a select group of patients, then we can start expanding it.
V/O:
Sam and Peter believe their work on the technique some are calling ‘suspended animation’ will in future save many lives. But, the procedure has opened a Pandora’s box of questions about life and death.
Peter:
It is a little bit daunting to know that what we used to call dead is not necessarily dead.

V/O: This is called an emergency resuscitative thoracotomy. Doctors clamp the aorta to preserve blood for the brain and heart and then try to repair the wounds. Peter: If it works you survive, if it doesn’t work we haven’t lost anything. This is us repairing the hole in his heart. V/O: This man survived. However, the survival rate using this last resort technique in military and civilian settings is very, very low. Sam: Peter Rhee did a review some fifteen years ago and the total was around seven percent. So it’s pretty bad, we can’t save many of them. In theory, if you had something novel, something new you could do, you might have been able to save some time to save them. What we do now doesn’t work, we’re losing patients daily and we got to try something different. V/O: Something different would be finding a way to suspend life to give surgeons more time to repair the injuries causing the bleeding. And the only way to buy more time is to find a way to protect the brain against the effects of blood loss. Both Sam and Peter have interacted with Dr Peter Safar. He is the man who developed CPR in the nineteen fifties and is known as the father of critical care. He once suggested a revolutionary way to go about protecting the brain – through hypothermia. This became the basis for what Peter and Sam have been working on for the last decade and a half. Peter: Instead of trying to fix the hole that was bleeding, can we buy ourselves maybe an hour of time by preserving the brain, by cooling it real fast and then while we are fixing the holes that are bleeding, bring the patient back up later on over slower time periods? V/O: Buying time by cooling a patient down made sense to them. It is a known fact that when the brain is cooled down, brain damage is limited. LINK: There are also many instances of people who drown in ice cold water, but then go on to survive the ordeal with little or no brain damage. V/O: Brain and heart surgeons also cool patients down as part of procedures that require that blood circulation be stopped for some time. Hypothermia seems to be the critical factor. Sam: Hypothermia basically affects every cell, every enzyme in the body and basically slows everything down. So cells require less energy, organs require less energy and thereby the need for oxygen, the need for blood flow that brings oxygen to the tissues goes down with the temperature. So the lower the temperature, the less oxygen is needed. LINK: This meant that if they could find a way to cool a victim down rapidly, the all the vital organs, including the brain, would require much less oxygen. V/O: And at these very low temperatures the brain can survive—even without oxygen—for some time. The big question became: could they cool somebody down rapidly in a trauma situation? After obtaining permission to carry out a study on pigs they were able to carefully operate on the animals and determine whether their unusual methods would have the expected results. This pig’s heart has just stopped beating. To cool the whole body down rapidly they pump a freezing cold salt water solution directly into the animal’s aorta. Peter: When we get into the blood stream and we pump and infuse cold saline into the body, we can cool every cell in the brain down very, very quickly. LINK: The cold saline solution replaced the blood of the animals and this lowered their body temperatures quickly and drastically. Peter: These were animals that were technically dead for anything from an hour to three hours. They had no blood in their body, they were at ten degrees. V/O: This very low temperature ensured that the animals sustained no brain damage and bought the surgeons more than enough time to fix all the damaged vessels that caused the bleeding. Once repairs had been finalised, they connected the animals to a heart lung machine and slowly warmed them up by replacing the cold saline with blood. Their first attempt was utterly nerve wracking. Peter: I’ll never forget that day. I’ll never forget that day. I remember distinctly we were all in the laboratory. There was a whole bunch of doctors and nurses and people in there. And when I warmed that pig back up and the heart started moving after it had been dead for well over an hour and a half. With no blood, cold, full of potassium solutions. But when that heart started to beat back up again, I could feel the hair on my neck going up and I almost felt like what Frankenstein would have felt like when he was doing his experiments. Link: And what is more, none of the animals sustained brain damage. Sam: So the function seems to be normal. We can actually look at their brains. We can have pathologists look to see if there is any brain damage. So as best as we could tell from the function, the pathologist says they look normal. Peter: So that where we are at now. We are at a phase where the science is good enough that we think we can try it in humans. LINK: Sam and his team have applied to the FDA to conduct human trials on 10 people in Pittsburgh. The application has been approved and trials are set to start very soon. Sam: Right now we just want to show that is can work. If we can show it works in a select group of patients, then we can start expanding it. V/O: Sam and Peter believe their work on the technique some are calling ‘suspended animation’ will in future save many lives. But, the procedure has opened a Pandora’s box of questions about life and death. Peter: It is a little bit daunting to know that what we used to call dead is not necessarily dead.

metadata.Summary: NEITHER dead or alive, knife-wound or gunshot victims will be cooled down and placed in suspended animation, as a groundbreaking emergency technique is tested out for the first time.
metadata.Further information: GUNSHOT VICTIMS TO BE SUSPENDED BETWEEN LIFE AND DEATH Doctors will try to save the lives of patients with knife or gunshot wounds by placing them in suspended animation, buying time to fix their injuries No heartbeat, no hope? No heartbeat, no hope? NEITHER dead or alive, knife-wound or gunshot victims will be cooled down and placed in suspended animation, as a groundbreaking emergency technique is tested out for the first time. Surgeons are now on call at the UPMC Presbyterian Hospital in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to perform the operation, which will buy doctors time to fix injuries that would otherwise be lethal. “We are suspending life, but we don’t like to call it suspended animation because it sounds like science fiction,” says Samuel Tisherman, a surgeon at the hospital, who is leading the trial. “So we call it emergency preservation and resuscitation.” The technique involves replacing all of a patient’s blood with a cold saline solution, which rapidly cools the body and stops almost all cellular activity. “If a patient comes to us two hours after dying you can’t bring them back to life. But if they’re dying and you suspend them, you have a chance to bring them back after their structural problems have been fixed,” says surgeon Peter Rhee at the University of Arizona in Tucson, who helped develop the technique. The benefits of cooling, or induced hypothermia, have been known for decades. At normal body temperature – around 37 °C – cells need a regular oxygen supply to produce energy. When the heart stops beating, blood no longer carries oxygen to cells. Without oxygen the brain can only survive for about 5 minutes before the damage is irreversible. However, at lower temperatures, cells need less oxygen because all chemical reactions slow down. This explains why people who fall into icy lakes can sometimes be revived more than half an hour after they have stopped breathing. Just before heart and brain surgery, doctors sometimes lower body temperature using ice packs, and by circulating the blood through an external cooling system. This can give them up to 45 minutes in which to stop blood flow and perform surgery. However, the cooling process takes time and can only be done with careful planning and preparation. When someone reaches an emergency department with a traumatic gunshot injury or stab wound, slow cooling isn’t an option. Often their heart has stopped beating due to extreme blood loss, giving doctors only minutes to stop the bleeding and restart the heart. Even if the bleeding can be stopped, it’s not like filling up an empty gas tank. Resuscitation exposes the body to a sudden onslaught of oxygen, which can cause tissues to release chemicals that damage cells and cause fatal “reperfusion” injuries. Finding ways to cool the body until it reaches a state of suspended animation – where people are not alive but not yet dead – could give doctors more time in an emergency. The technique was first demonstrated in pigs in 2000 by Rhee and his colleagues. The animals were sedated and a massive haemorrhage induced, to mimic the effect of multiple gunshot wounds. Their blood was drained and replaced by either a cold potassium or saline solution, rapidly cooling the body to around 10 °C. After the injuries were treated, the animals were gradually warmed up as the solution was replaced with blood. Vital signs The pig’s heart usually started beating again by itself, although some pigs needed a jump-start. There was no effect on physical or cognitive function (Surgery, doi.org/dvhdzs). “After we did those experiments, the definition of ‘dead’ changed,” says Rhee. “Every day at work I declare people dead. They have no signs of life, no heartbeat, no brain activity. I sign a piece of paper knowing in my heart that they are not actually dead. I could, right then and there, suspend them. But I have to put them in a body bag. It’s frustrating to know there’s a solution.” “I sign a piece of paper knowing in my heart that they are not actually dead. It’s frustrating” That solution will be put to the test in humans for the first time. A final meeting this week will ensure that a team of doctors is fully prepared to try it. Then all they have to do is wait for the right patient to arrive. That person will have suffered a cardiac arrest after a traumatic injury, and will not have responded to attempts to start their heart. When this happens, every member of Tisherman’s team will be paged. “The patient will probably have already lost about 50 per cent of their blood and their chest will be open,” he says. The team sees one of these cases each month. Their chance of survival is less than 7 per cent. The first step is to flush cold saline through the heart and up to the brain – the areas most vulnerable to low oxygen. To do this, the lower region of their heart must be clamped and a catheter placed into the aorta – the largest artery in the body – to carry the saline. The clamp is later removed so the saline can be artificially pumped around the whole body. It takes about 15 minutes for the patient’s temperature to drop to 10 °C. At this point they will have no blood in their body, no breathing, and no brain activity. They will be clinically dead. In this state, almost no metabolic reactions happen in the body, so cells can survive without oxygen. Instead, they may be producing energy through what’s called anaerobic glycolysis. At normal body temperatures this can sustain cells for about 2 minutes. At low temperatures, however, glycolysis rates are so low that cells can survive for hours. The patient will be disconnected from all machinery and taken to an operating room where surgeons have up to 2 hours to fix the injury. The saline is then replaced with blood. If the heart does not restart by itself, as it did in the pig trial, the patient is resuscitated. The new blood will heat the body slowly, which should help prevent any reperfusion injuries. The technique will be tested on 10 people, and the outcome compared with another 10 who met the criteria but who weren’t treated this way because the team wasn’t on hand. The technique will be refined then tested on another 10, says Tisherman, until there are enough results to analyse. “We’ve always assumed that you can’t bring back the dead. But it’s a matter of when you pickle the cells,” says Rhee. “Until now we had always assumed that you can’t bring people back from the dead” Getting this technique into hospitals hasn’t been easy. Because the trial will happen during a medical emergency, neither the patient nor their family can give consent. The trial can only go ahead because the US Food and Drug Administration considers it to be exempt from informed consent. That’s because it will involve people whose injuries are likely to be fatal and there is no alternative treatment. The team had to have discussions with groups in the community and place adverts in newspapers describing the trial. People can opt out online. So far, nobody has. Tisherman says he eventually hopes to extend the technique to other conditions. For now, suspended animation is limited to a few hours. But that’s not to say that more lengthy suspension isn’t possible (see “Will human hibernation ever happen“). “We’re trying to save lives, not pack people off to Mars,” says Tisherman. “Can we go longer than a few hours with no blood flow? I don’t know. Maybe years from now someone will have figured out how to do it, but it will certainly take time.”
